title: Song of Solomon 5:9–16
context: The Friends ask how her beloved is better than another (5:9), and the Beloved answers with a poem praising him from head to foot, ending, “This is my beloved, and this is my friend” (5:10–16). Allegorical readers have often heard this as praise of Christ; literal readers hear a bride’s admiration of her husband. Speaker assignments follow the WEB headings and are held as reasonable readings.

verses.text: How is your beloved better than another beloved, you fairest among women? How is your beloved better than another beloved, that you do so adjure us?
verses.arminianNotes: The WEB heading marks the Friends: “How is your beloved better than another beloved, you fairest among women?” Arminian readers see a question that invites the beloved to describe him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the question prompting the praise that follows. Allegorical readers often use it to ask what makes Christ incomparable, while literal readers see friends drawing out her affection.

verses.text: My beloved is white and ruddy. The best among ten thousand.
verses.arminianNotes: Under the heading Beloved: “My beloved is white and ruddy. The best among ten thousand.” Arminian readers see admiration for one who stands out among all others.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see praise of incomparable worth. Allegorical readers have often applied this to Christ’s excellence, while literal readers see a bride’s admiration of her husband; both approaches appear within this tradition.

verses.text: His head is like the purest gold. His hair is bushy, black as a raven.
verses.arminianNotes: “His head is like the purest gold. His hair is bushy, black as a raven.” Arminian readers see honor and strength expressed through images of gold and dark color.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see language of worth and vigor. Readers in this tradition caution against pressing each image symbolically, preferring to see the overall impression of excellence.

verses.text: His eyes are like doves beside the water brooks, washed with milk, mounted like jewels.
verses.arminianNotes: “His eyes are like doves beside the water brooks.” Arminian readers see gentleness and clarity praised, echoing the dove imagery used earlier for the beloved herself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see tenderness pictured. The repetition of dove imagery suggests mutual regard, whether the Song is read literally or allegorically.

verses.text: His cheeks are like a bed of spices with towers of perfumes. His lips are like lilies, dropping liquid myrrh.
verses.arminianNotes: “His cheeks are like a bed of spices … His lips are like lilies.” Arminian readers see fragrance and beauty used to describe a beloved whose presence is delightful.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see images of sweetness. Allegorical readers sometimes connect this with the gracious words of Christ, though literal readers see a bride’s affection; the text leaves both open.

verses.text: His hands are like rings of gold set with beryl. His body is like ivory work overlaid with sapphires.
verses.arminianNotes: “His hands are like rings of gold set with beryl.” Arminian readers see value and craftsmanship used to express admiration for the beloved’s strength and worth.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see images of precious materials. The identification of some gemstones named here is uncertain, and readers in this tradition do not press them.

verses.text: His legs are like pillars of marble set on sockets of fine gold. His appearance is like Lebanon, excellent as the cedars.
verses.arminianNotes: “His legs are like pillars of marble … His appearance is like Lebanon, excellent as the cedars.” Arminian readers see strength and stability praised.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see images of grandeur. The cedars of Lebanon symbolize majesty elsewhere in Scripture, and readers in this tradition see the image as conveying noble stature.

verses.text: His mouth is sweetness; yes, he is altogether lovely. This is my beloved, and this is my friend, daughters of Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: “… yes, he is altogether lovely. This is my beloved, and this is my friend, daughters of Jerusalem.” Arminian readers see love that combines delight and friendship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the climax of the beloved’s praise. Allegorical readers often apply “altogether lovely” to Christ, while literal readers see the friendship that belongs to married love.
